moa.mechanism: Bee venom contains melittin and other peptides, and the cosmetic rationale is that a controlled low-level irritation prompts a visible tightening response — essentially the same logic as a mild chemical stressor. Laboratory work on individual venom components exists; controlled work on cosmetic products at cosmetic levels is very thin. The important consideration is not efficacy but allergy: venom proteins can provoke serious reactions in sensitised people. Cosmetic-grade venom is heavily diluted, which reduces that concern without removing it, and no cosmetic dilution makes a known bee allergy safe to test at home.
moa.ceiling: Unproven cosmetically, and genuinely unsuitable for anyone with a bee allergy. Ask a doctor first.

moa.target: oil and debris on the skin surface
moa.mechanism: Activated charcoal is carbon processed to create an enormous porous surface area, which lets it adsorb molecules onto that surface. In water treatment this is genuinely powerful. On skin, in a mask worn for a few minutes, it can pick up some surface oil and residue. It cannot reach inside a pore, and adsorption of a substance onto carbon is not the same thing as drawing anything out of skin.
moa.ceiling: Surface pick-up only. There is no detoxification, and peel-off versions mainly remove fine facial hair.

moa.target: removing oil and grime while keeping skin comfortable
moa.mechanism: Sodium cocoyl glutamate is an anionic surfactant built from coconut-derived fatty acids and the amino acid glutamic acid. Its molecules surround oils so they can be rinsed away, but they are milder toward skin proteins and lipids than sulfates, and the class works at a pH close to skin's own rather than the high pH of true soap. That combination is why an amino acid cleanser leaves less of the tight, squeaky feeling.
moa.ceiling: A gentle cleanser. It does not treat acne, and it foams less than a sulfate by design.

moa.target: surface softening and water loss
moa.mechanism: Meadowfoam seed oil is dominated by unusually long-chain fatty acids, giving it a composition closer to a liquid wax than a conventional triglyceride oil. That structure makes it exceptionally resistant to oxidation and gives a light cushioning film on the surface that slows evaporation. It behaves, in practice, much like jojoba: a stable, pleasant emollient chosen for reliability rather than for any active property. That stability is why it turns up in balms and cleansing oils meant to sit on a shelf for a long time, where a more delicate seed oil would quietly go off.
moa.ceiling: An emollient. There is no evidence it does anything beyond softening and sealing.

moa.target: surface comfort and barrier lipids
moa.mechanism: Sunflower seed oil is high in linoleic acid, the essential fatty acid that skin uses in building the lipids between surface cells and which tends to be relatively low in dry and acne-prone skin. Applied topically it softens the surface and slows water loss, and linoleic-rich oils have been studied for barrier comfort with more supportive results than most cosmetic oils manage. Refined, fresh oil matters — oxidised oil is an irritant.
moa.ceiling: A supportive emollient. It does not replace ceramides or treat any skin condition.

conflicts.reason: Retinised skin stings under a high-alcohol formula. Keep the quick-dry sunscreen for mornings and the retinal for nights, and stop stacking them in one step.
Freshly exfoliated skin is the least forgiving surface for a solvent-heavy formula. Space them, or choose a lower-alcohol sunscreen on acid days.
Astringent distillates on retinised skin is a reliable route to stinging and visible redness. Pick one; the retinol is the one doing the work.
Both strip and tighten, and the combination is a classic cause of skin that looks calm for an hour and reacts for a week.
Ascorbic derivatives can destabilise copper peptide complexes. Separate them — vitamin C in the morning, peptides at night.
Not dangerous, just badly matched in one layer. Morning for the vitamin C derivative, evening for the retinal.
The old vitamin C and niacinamide warning came from a study using heat and raw ascorbic acid. With a stable derivative in a finished formula it does not apply.
Deliberately combined. Filters are blended to cover more of the spectrum and to keep each other stable in sunlight.
Both are bee-derived. If either has ever caused you a reaction, treat the other as suspect too, and ask a doctor if you have a known bee allergy.
A clay mask and an acid on the same evening is the most common way people talk themselves into a stripped, stinging face. Choose one per night.
Both target oil, and doubling up on a blemish is how a spot becomes a dry, flaking patch that lasts longer than the spot would have.
The intended pairing. A humectant supplies the water, an occlusive keeps it there — mineral oil over a hydrating layer, never over bare dry skin.
